newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Greek minister skeptical about U.N. talks on Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Greek minister skeptical about U.N. talks on Cyprus.

text.p: Greece's deputy foreign minister said on Tuesday he was not optimistic about planned U.N.-sponsored talks on Cyprus but that Secretary-General Kofi Annan should be encouraged in his initiative.
Yannos Kranidiotis also told a news conference he believed the talks would take place in early or mid-July but that no definite date had been set yet. U.N. officials earlier had hoped for June date.
He said little common ground had been found in so-called "proximity" or separate talks between U.N. officials and Cypriot leaders earlier this year.
"I cannot say that I am very optimistic about the talks, he said after speaking to Annan about Cyprus.

"However, I believe the effort should be made and we should all try and help to find a solution. Things would have been much easier if common ground had been found during the proximity talks," he said.
"Unless Turkey realises that it has to make concessions, the prospects are not very good," he added.

Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when troops from Turkey took over the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece. The United Nations has been trying for more than 20 years to reunite the Greek and Turkish Cypriots under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federal system.
If the talks do get off the ground, it would be the first known encounter between Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides, as head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

Kranidiotis blamed the lack of progress on "Turkish intransigence and the Turkish negative approach to the Cyprus problem," adding that the international community had to put pressure on Turkey to give ground.

But at the same time he said Greece had doubts about a bi-zonal, bi-communal federal system which U.N. members had advocated. "We believe this state should be functional, viable... with a strong central authority which would security the unity of the state," he said.
The minister also repeatedly emphasised Cyprus' prospective full membership in the European Community, saying this appreciably "changed the picture."
"Any effort for a Cyprus solution should take into account of this new element," he said. This included ideas the United Nations presented in 1992, which he now called "obsolete."
"Full membership of Cyprus in the European Union should be part of the solution," he said.
